D003_l001.question:
A 27-year-old single female architectural designer presents with a 2-year-2-month history of prominent hyperactive and impulsive behaviors accompanied by longstanding attentional difficulties. Symptoms reportedly began in childhood, with onset prior to age 12, but have become more impairing in her current occupational role.

She describes persistent motor restlessness, including frequent fidgeting with hands and feet when seated and difficulty remaining seated in settings where this is expected (e.g., meetings). She reports an internal sense of restlessness and feeling “on the go,” with difficulty relaxing. In work discussions she tends to respond prematurely before questions are fully posed and struggles to wait her turn in conversations and group settings.

Inattention symptoms include difficulty sustaining focus on detailed or prolonged tasks, leading to frequent shifts between projects. She reports problems following through on instructions and incomplete work tasks unless provided with external structure or reminders. She also notes chronic disorganization, with challenges planning, prioritizing, and managing multiple deadlines.

These symptoms cause significant functional impairment in occupational performance and in social and team-based interactions. There is no indication that demographic factors such as her occupational status or marital status temporally precipitated the symptom onset.
D003_l001.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D003_l002.question:
A 37-year-old married male university admissions officer presents with a 2-year-2-month history of prominent hyperactive and impulsive behaviors along with attentional difficulties, causing significant impairment in occupational and daily functioning. He reports persistent motor restlessness, including frequent fidgeting and difficulty remaining seated during meetings or extended desk work. He experiences an internal sense of restlessness and difficulty staying physically still in settings that require sustained inactivity. In conversations and meetings, he tends to interject prematurely and respond before questions are fully posed, and he has notable difficulty waiting his turn in group discussions or queues.

Cognitively, the patient describes marked difficulty maintaining concentration on routine or prolonged tasks, with frequent lapses in attention during application reviews and administrative duties. He has recurrent problems following through on assigned tasks and completing work responsibilities in a timely manner. Organizational skills are impaired, with trouble structuring tasks, managing deadlines, and maintaining orderly workflows, leading to errors, inefficiency, and increased stress in the workplace and at home.
D003_l002.options:
A. Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
    B. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation)
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
